# Lucas sequence

 [Edit links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q1759646#sitelinks-wikipedia)                          From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia   Certain constant-recursive integer sequences Not to be confused with the sequence of [Lucas numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_number), which is a particular Lucas sequence.

In [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), the **Lucas sequences**      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}   are certain [constant-recursive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constant-recursive_sequence) [integer sequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_sequence) that satisfy the [recurrence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrence_relation)

      x  n   = P ⋅  x  n − 1   − Q ⋅  x  n − 2     {\displaystyle x_{n}=P\cdot x_{n-1}-Q\cdot x_{n-2}}

where     P   {\displaystyle P}   and     Q   {\displaystyle Q}   are fixed [integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer). Although      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}   satisfy the same recurrence relation, they differ on the values of their first two elements and thus differ for subsequent elements as well. Any sequence satisfying this recurrence relation can be represented as a [linear combination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_combination) of the Lucas sequences      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q ) .   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q).}

More generally, Lucas sequences      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}   represent sequences of [polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial) in     P   {\displaystyle P}   and     Q   {\displaystyle Q}   with integer [coefficients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coefficient).

Famous examples of Lucas sequences include the [Fibonacci numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_number), [Mersenne numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mersenne_number), [Pell numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell_number), [Lucas numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_number), [Jacobsthal numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobsthal_number), and a superset of [Fermat numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_number) (see below). Lucas sequences are named after the [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France) mathematician [Édouard Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89douard_Lucas).

## Recurrence relations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=1)]

Given two integer parameters     P   {\displaystyle P}   and     Q   {\displaystyle Q}  , the Lucas sequences of the first kind      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and of the second kind      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}   are defined by the [recurrence relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrence_relation):

          U  0   ( P , Q )    = 0 ,      U  1   ( P , Q )    = 1 ,      U  n   ( P , Q )    = P ⋅  U  n − 1   ( P , Q ) − Q ⋅  U  n − 2   ( P , Q )    for    n > 1 ,       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}U_{0}(P,Q)&=0,\\U_{1}(P,Q)&=1,\\U_{n}(P,Q)&=P\cdot U_{n-1}(P,Q)-Q\cdot U_{n-2}(P,Q){\mbox{ for }}n>1,\end{aligned}}}

and

          V  0   ( P , Q )    = 2 ,      V  1   ( P , Q )    = P ,      V  n   ( P , Q )    = P ⋅  V  n − 1   ( P , Q ) − Q ⋅  V  n − 2   ( P , Q )    for    n > 1.       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}V_{0}(P,Q)&=2,\\V_{1}(P,Q)&=P,\\V_{n}(P,Q)&=P\cdot V_{n-1}(P,Q)-Q\cdot V_{n-2}(P,Q){\mbox{ for }}n>1.\end{aligned}}}

It is not hard to show that for     n > 0   {\displaystyle n>0}  ,

          U  n   ( P , Q )    =    P ⋅  U  n − 1   ( P , Q ) +  V  n − 1   ( P , Q )  2   ,      V  n   ( P , Q )    =    (  P  2   − 4 Q ) ⋅  U  n − 1   ( P , Q ) + P ⋅  V  n − 1   ( P , Q )  2   .       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}U_{n}(P,Q)&={\frac {P\cdot U_{n-1}(P,Q)+V_{n-1}(P,Q)}{2}},\\V_{n}(P,Q)&={\frac {(P^{2}-4Q)\cdot U_{n-1}(P,Q)+P\cdot V_{n-1}(P,Q)}{2}}.\end{aligned}}}

The above relations can be stated in [matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) form as follows:

       [     U  n   ( P , Q )      U  n + 1   ( P , Q )    ]   =   [    0   1     − Q   P    ]   ⋅   [     U  n − 1   ( P , Q )      U  n   ( P , Q )    ]   ,   {\displaystyle {\begin{bmatrix}U_{n}(P,Q)\\U_{n+1}(P,Q)\end{bmatrix}}={\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-Q&P\end{bmatrix}}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}U_{n-1}(P,Q)\\U_{n}(P,Q)\end{bmatrix}},}

       [     V  n   ( P , Q )      V  n + 1   ( P , Q )    ]   =   [    0   1     − Q   P    ]   ⋅   [     V  n − 1   ( P , Q )      V  n   ( P , Q )    ]   ,   {\displaystyle {\begin{bmatrix}V_{n}(P,Q)\\V_{n+1}(P,Q)\end{bmatrix}}={\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-Q&P\end{bmatrix}}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}V_{n-1}(P,Q)\\V_{n}(P,Q)\end{bmatrix}},}

       [     U  n   ( P , Q )      V  n   ( P , Q )    ]   =   [    P  /  2   1  /  2     (  P  2   − 4 Q )  /  2   P  /  2    ]   ⋅   [     U  n − 1   ( P , Q )      V  n − 1   ( P , Q )    ]   .   {\displaystyle {\begin{bmatrix}U_{n}(P,Q)\\V_{n}(P,Q)\end{bmatrix}}={\begin{bmatrix}P/2&1/2\\(P^{2}-4Q)/2&P/2\end{bmatrix}}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}U_{n-1}(P,Q)\\V_{n-1}(P,Q)\end{bmatrix}}.}

Initial terms of Lucas sequences      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}   are given in the table:

         n    U  n   ( P , Q )    V  n   ( P , Q )     0   0   2     1   1   P     2   P     P   2   − 2 Q     3     P   2   − Q     P   3   − 3 P Q     4     P   3   − 2 P Q     P   4   − 4   P   2   Q + 2   Q   2       5     P   4   − 3   P   2   Q +   Q   2       P   5   − 5   P   3   Q + 5 P   Q   2       6     P   5   − 4   P   3   Q + 3 P   Q   2       P   6   − 6   P   4   Q + 9   P   2     Q   2   − 2   Q   3         {\displaystyle {\begin{array}{r|l|l}n&U_{n}(P,Q)&V_{n}(P,Q)\\\hline 0&0&2\\1&1&P\\2&P&{P}^{2}-2Q\\3&{P}^{2}-Q&{P}^{3}-3PQ\\4&{P}^{3}-2PQ&{P}^{4}-4{P}^{2}Q+2{Q}^{2}\\5&{P}^{4}-3{P}^{2}Q+{Q}^{2}&{P}^{5}-5{P}^{3}Q+5P{Q}^{2}\\6&{P}^{5}-4{P}^{3}Q+3P{Q}^{2}&{P}^{6}-6{P}^{4}Q+9{P}^{2}{Q}^{2}-2{Q}^{3}\end{array}}}

## Explicit expressions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=2)]

The characteristic equation of the recurrence relation for Lucas sequences      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}   is:

      x  2   − P x + Q = 0    {\displaystyle x^{2}-Px+Q=0\,}

It has the [discriminant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discriminant)     D =  P  2   − 4 Q   {\displaystyle D=P^{2}-4Q}   and, by the [quadratic formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_formula), has the [roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_of_a_polynomial):

     a =    P +   D    2     and   b =    P −   D    2   .    {\displaystyle a={\frac {P+{\sqrt {D}}}{2}}\quad {\text{and}}\quad b={\frac {P-{\sqrt {D}}}{2}}.\,}

Thus:

     a + b = P  ,   {\displaystyle a+b=P\,,}       a b =   1 4   (  P  2   − D ) = Q  ,   {\displaystyle ab={\frac {1}{4}}(P^{2}-D)=Q\,,}       a − b =   D    .   {\displaystyle a-b={\sqrt {D}}\,.}

Note that the sequence      a  n     {\displaystyle a^{n}}   and the sequence      b  n     {\displaystyle b^{n}}   also satisfy the recurrence relation. However these might not be integer sequences.

### Distinct roots

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=3)]

When     D ≠ 0   {\displaystyle D\neq 0}  , *a* and *b* are distinct and one quickly verifies that

      a  n   =     V  n   +  U  n     D    2     {\displaystyle a^{n}={\frac {V_{n}+U_{n}{\sqrt {D}}}{2}}}        b  n   =     V  n   −  U  n     D    2   .   {\displaystyle b^{n}={\frac {V_{n}-U_{n}{\sqrt {D}}}{2}}.}

It follows that the terms of Lucas sequences can be expressed in terms of *a* and *b* as follows

      U  n   =     a  n   −  b  n     a − b    =     a  n   −  b  n     D      {\displaystyle U_{n}={\frac {a^{n}-b^{n}}{a-b}}={\frac {a^{n}-b^{n}}{\sqrt {D}}}}        V  n   =  a  n   +  b  n      {\displaystyle V_{n}=a^{n}+b^{n}\,}

### Repeated root

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=4)]

The case     D = 0   {\displaystyle D=0}   occurs exactly when     P = 2 S   and   Q =  S  2     {\displaystyle P=2S{\text{ and }}Q=S^{2}}   for some integer *S* so that     a = b = S   {\displaystyle a=b=S}  . In this case one easily finds that

      U  n   ( P , Q ) =  U  n   ( 2 S ,  S  2   ) = n  S  n − 1      {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)=U_{n}(2S,S^{2})=nS^{n-1}\,}        V  n   ( P , Q ) =  V  n   ( 2 S ,  S  2   ) = 2  S  n   .    {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)=V_{n}(2S,S^{2})=2S^{n}.\,}

## Properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=5)]

### Generating functions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=6)]

The ordinary [generating functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generating_function) are

      ∑  n ≥ 0    U  n   ( P , Q )  z  n   =   z  1 − P z + Q  z  2      ;   {\displaystyle \sum _{n\geq 0}U_{n}(P,Q)z^{n}={\frac {z}{1-Pz+Qz^{2}}};}        ∑  n ≥ 0    V  n   ( P , Q )  z  n   =    2 − P z   1 − P z + Q  z  2      .   {\displaystyle \sum _{n\geq 0}V_{n}(P,Q)z^{n}={\frac {2-Pz}{1-Pz+Qz^{2}}}.}

### Pell equations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=7)]

When     Q = ± 1   {\displaystyle Q=\pm 1}  , the Lucas sequences      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}   satisfy certain [Pell equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell_equation):

      V  n   ( P , 1  )  2   − D ⋅  U  n   ( P , 1  )  2   = 4 ,   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,1)^{2}-D\cdot U_{n}(P,1)^{2}=4,}        V  n   ( P , − 1  )  2   − D ⋅  U  n   ( P , − 1  )  2   = 4 ( − 1  )  n   .   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,-1)^{2}-D\cdot U_{n}(P,-1)^{2}=4(-1)^{n}.}

### Relations between sequences with different parameters

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=8)]
- For any number *c*, the sequences      U  n   (  P ′  ,  Q ′  )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P',Q')}   and      V  n   (  P ′  ,  Q ′  )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P',Q')}   with
      P ′  = P + 2 c   {\displaystyle P'=P+2c}        Q ′  = c P + Q +  c  2     {\displaystyle Q'=cP+Q+c^{2}}   have the same discriminant as      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}  :      P  ′  2    − 4  Q ′  = ( P + 2 c  )  2   − 4 ( c P + Q +  c  2   ) =  P  2   − 4 Q = D .   {\displaystyle P'^{2}-4Q'=(P+2c)^{2}-4(cP+Q+c^{2})=P^{2}-4Q=D.}
- For any number *c*, we also have
      U  n   ( c P ,  c  2   Q ) =  c  n − 1   ⋅  U  n   ( P , Q ) ,   {\displaystyle U_{n}(cP,c^{2}Q)=c^{n-1}\cdot U_{n}(P,Q),}        V  n   ( c P ,  c  2   Q ) =  c  n   ⋅  V  n   ( P , Q ) .   {\displaystyle V_{n}(cP,c^{2}Q)=c^{n}\cdot V_{n}(P,Q).}

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=9)]

{L_{m}L_{n}+5F_{m}F_{n}}{2}}&(9)\\V_{n}^{2}-DU_{n}^{2}=4Q^{n}&L_{n}^{2}-5F_{n}^{2}=4(-1)^{n}&(10)\\U_{n}^{2}-U_{n-1}U_{n+1}=Q^{n-1}&F_{n}^{2}-F_{n-1}F_{n+1}=(-1)^{n-1}&(11)\\V_{n}^{2}-V_{n-1}V_{n+1}=DQ^{n-1}&L_{n}^{2}-L_{n-1}L_{n+1}=5(-1)^{n-1}&(12)\\2^{n-1}U_{n}={n \choose 1}P^{n-1}+{n \choose 3}P^{n-3}D+\cdots &2^{n-1}F_{n}={n \choose 1}+5{n \choose 3}+\cdots &(13)\\2^{n-1}V_{n}=P^{n}+{n \choose 2}P^{n-2}D+{n \choose 4}P^{n-4}D^{2}+\cdots &2^{n-1}L_{n}=1+5{n \choose 2}+5^{2}{n \choose 4}+\cdots &(14)\end{array}}}

#### Fast computation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=10)]

Various analogues of [exponentiation by squaring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponentiation_by_squaring) can be used to calculate Lucas sequences efficiently, in ⁠      O   ( log ⁡ n )   {\displaystyle {\mathcal {O}}(\log n)}  ⁠ operations. To simultaneously calculate      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}  , one can use the properties (3) and (4) to perform double-and-add. Alternatively, calculate the matrix exponentiation      M  n   =   (        0   1     − Q   P        )     {\displaystyle M^{n}={\big (}{\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-Q&P\end{smallmatrix}}{\big )}}   to use       (          U  n          U  n + 1           )   =  M  n     (        0     1        )     {\displaystyle {\big (}{\begin{smallmatrix}{U_{n}}\\{U_{n+1}}\end{smallmatrix}}{\big )}=M^{n}{\big (}{\begin{smallmatrix}0\\1\end{smallmatrix}}{\big )}}   and       (          V  n          V  n + 1           )   =  M  n     (        2     P        )   .   {\displaystyle {\big (}{\begin{smallmatrix}{V_{n}}\\{V_{n+1}}\end{smallmatrix}}{\big )}=M^{n}{\big (}{\begin{smallmatrix}2\\P\end{smallmatrix}}{\big )}.}

(6) and (7) allow fast calculation of *V* independent of *U* using double-and-add. The relation      V  m n   =  V  m   ( P =  V  n   , Q =  Q  n   )   {\displaystyle V_{mn}=V_{m}(P=V_{n},Q=Q_{n})}   (which belongs to the section above, "relations between sequences with different parameters") is also useful for this purpose.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-1)

Another ⁠      O   ( log ⁡ n )   {\displaystyle {\mathcal {O}}(\log n)}  ⁠ method based on (3) and (6) is the [Lucas chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_chain). This method takes fewer operations than double-and-add but requires pre-calculation of chains.

### Divisibility properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=11)]

Among the consequences is that      U  k m   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{km}(P,Q)}   is a multiple of      U  m   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{m}(P,Q)}  , i.e., the sequence     (  U  m   ( P , Q )  )  m ≥ 1     {\displaystyle (U_{m}(P,Q))_{m\geq 1}}   is a [divisibility sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisibility_sequence). This implies, in particular, that      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   can be [prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number) only when *n* is prime. Moreover, if     gcd ( P , Q ) = 1   {\displaystyle \gcd(P,Q)=1}  , then     (  U  m   ( P , Q )  )  m ≥ 1     {\displaystyle (U_{m}(P,Q))_{m\geq 1}}   is a [strong divisibility sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisibility_sequence).

Other divisibility properties are as follows:[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-2)

- If *n* is an [odd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parity_(mathematics)) multiple of *m*, then      V  m     {\displaystyle V_{m}}   divides      V  n     {\displaystyle V_{n}}  .
- Let *N* be an integer [relatively prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relatively_prime) to 2*Q*. If the smallest positive integer *r* for which *N* divides      U  r     {\displaystyle U_{r}}   exists, then the set of *n* for which *N* divides      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   is exactly the set of multiples of *r*.
- If *P* and *Q* are [even](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parity_(mathematics)), then      U  n   ,  V  n     {\displaystyle U_{n},V_{n}}   are always even except      U  1     {\displaystyle U_{1}}  .
- If *P* is odd and *Q* is even, then      U  n   ,  V  n     {\displaystyle U_{n},V_{n}}   are always odd for every     n > 0   {\displaystyle n>0}  .
- If *P* is even and *Q* is odd, then the [parity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parity_(mathematics)) of      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   is the same as *n* and      V  n     {\displaystyle V_{n}}   is always even.
- If *P* and *Q* are odd, then      U  n   ,  V  n     {\displaystyle U_{n},V_{n}}   are even if and only if *n* is a multiple of 3.
- If *p* is an odd prime, then      U  p   ≡  (    D p    )  ,  V  p   ≡ P   ( mod  p )    {\displaystyle U_{p}\equiv \left({\tfrac {D}{p}}\right),V_{p}\equiv P{\pmod {p}}}   (see [Legendre symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre_symbol)).
- If *p* is an odd prime which divides *P* and *Q*, then *p* divides      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   for every     n > 1   {\displaystyle n>1}  .
- If *p* is an odd prime which divides *P* but not *Q*, then *p* divides      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   if and only if *n* is even.
- If *p* is an odd prime which divides *Q* but not *P*, then *p* never divides      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   for any     n > 0   {\displaystyle n>0}  .
- If *p* is an odd prime which divides *D* but not *PQ*, then *p* divides      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   if and only if *p* divides *n*.
- If *p* is an odd prime which does not divide *PQD*, then *p* divides      U  l     {\displaystyle U_{l}}  , where     l = p −  (    D p    )    {\displaystyle l=p-\left({\tfrac {D}{p}}\right)}  .

The last fact generalizes [Fermat's little theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat's_little_theorem). These facts are used in the [Lucas–Lehmer primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas%E2%80%93Lehmer_primality_test). Like Fermat's little theorem, the [converse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Converse_(logic)) of the last fact holds often, but not always; there exist [composite numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_number) *n* relatively prime to *D* and dividing      U  l     {\displaystyle U_{l}}  , where     l = n −  (    D n    )    {\displaystyle l=n-\left({\tfrac {D}{n}}\right)}  . Such composite numbers are called [Lucas pseudoprimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_pseudoprime).

A [prime factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_factor) of a term in a Lucas sequence which does not divide any earlier term in the sequence is called **primitive**. [Carmichael's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael's_theorem) states that all but finitely many of the terms in a Lucas sequence have a primitive prime factor.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-Yabuta-3) Indeed, [Carmichael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Daniel_Carmichael) (1913) showed that if *D* is positive and *n* is not 1, 2 or 6, then      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   has a primitive prime factor. In the case *D* is negative, a deep result of Bilu, Hanrot, Voutier and Mignotte[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-4) shows that if *n* > 30, then      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   has a primitive prime factor and determines all cases      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   has no primitive prime factor.

## Specific names

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=12)]

The Lucas sequences for some values of *P* and *Q* have specific names:

 *Un*(1, −1) : [Fibonacci numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_number) *Vn*(1, −1) : [Lucas numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_number) *Un*(2, −1) : [Pell numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell_number) *Vn*(2, −1) : [Pell–Lucas numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell%E2%80%93Lucas_numbers) (companion Pell numbers) *Un*(2, 1) : [Counting numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counting_numbers) *Un*(1, −2) : [Jacobsthal numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobsthal_number) *Vn*(1, −2) : [Jacobsthal–Lucas numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobsthal%E2%80%93Lucas_numbers) *Un*(3, 2) : [Mersenne numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mersenne_number) 2*n* − 1 *Vn*(3, 2) : Numbers of the form 2*n* + 1, which include the [Fermat numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_number)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-Yabuta-3) *Un*(6, 1) : The square roots of the [square triangular numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_triangular_number). *Un*(*x*, −1) : [Fibonacci polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_polynomials) *Vn*(*x*, −1) : [Lucas polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_polynomials) *Un*(2*x*, 1) : [Chebyshev polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebyshev_polynomials) of second kind *Vn*(2*x*, 1) : [Chebyshev polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebyshev_polynomials) of first kind multiplied by 2 *Un*(*x* + 1, *x*) : [Repunits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repunit) in base *x* *Vn*(*x* + 1, *x*) : *x**n* + 1

## Applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=13)]
- Lucas sequences are used in probabilistic [Lucas pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_pseudoprime) tests, which are part of the commonly used [Baillie–PSW primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baillie%E2%80%93PSW_primality_test).
- Lucas sequences are used in some primality proof methods, including the [Lucas–Lehmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas%E2%80%93Lehmer_primality_test) and [Lucas–Lehmer–Riesel tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas%E2%80%93Lehmer%E2%80%93Riesel_test) and the hybrid N−1/N+1 methods such as those in Brillhart-Lehmer-Selfridge 1975.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-BLS75-6)
- LUC is a [public-key cryptosystem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public-key_cryptosystem) based on Lucas sequences[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-7) that implements the analogs of [ElGamal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ElGamal) (LUCELG), [Diffie–Hellman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffie%E2%80%93Hellman) (LUCDIF), and [RSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(algorithm)) (LUCRSA). The encryption of the message in LUC is computed as a term of certain Lucas sequence, instead of using [modular exponentiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_exponentiation) as in RSA or Diffie–Hellman. However, it is argued[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-8) that many of the supposed security advantages of LUC over cryptosystems based on modular exponentiation are either not present, or not as substantial as claimed.

## Generalizations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=14)]

The sequence      V  n   ( P , Q ) =  a  n   +  b  n     {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)=a^{n}+b^{n}}  , which is a solution to the recurrence      V  n   ( P , Q ) = P  V  n − 1   ( P , Q ) − Q  V  n − 2   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)=PV_{n-1}(P,Q)-QV_{n-2}(P,Q)}   when ⁠    a   {\displaystyle a}  ⁠ and ⁠    b   {\displaystyle b}  ⁠ are the roots of the corresponding quadratic equation ⁠     z  2   − P z + Q = 0   {\displaystyle z^{2}-Pz+Q=0}  ⁠, generalizes to degree ⁠    k ≥ 1   {\displaystyle k\geq 1}  ⁠. Specifically, for the recurrence relation      V  n   (  P  1   , … ,  P  k   ) =  ∑  j = 1   k    P  j    V  n − j   (  P  1   , … ,  P  k   )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P_{1},\ldots ,P_{k})=\sum _{j=1}^{k}P_{j}V_{n-j}(P_{1},\ldots ,P_{k})}   with integers ⁠     P  1   , … ,  P  k     {\displaystyle P_{1},\ldots ,P_{k}}  ⁠ and typically with ⁠     P  k   ≠ 0   {\displaystyle P_{k}\neq 0}  ⁠, let ⁠     a  1   , … ,  a  k     {\displaystyle a_{1},\ldots ,a_{k}}  ⁠ be the roots of the corresponding polynomial equation      z  k   −  ∑  j = 1   k    P  j    z  k − j   = 0.   {\displaystyle z^{k}-\sum _{j=1}^{k}P_{j}z^{k-j}=0.}   Then      V  n   (  P  1   , … ,  P  k   ) =  ∑  j = 1   k    a  j   n     {\displaystyle V_{n}(P_{1},\ldots ,P_{k})=\sum _{j=1}^{k}a_{j}^{n}}   is a sequence of integers satisfying the recurrence, as is evidenced by its [ordinary generating function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinary_generating_function),      G   P  1   , … ,  P  k     ( z ) =  ∑  n = 0   ∞    V  n   (  P  1   , … ,  P  k   )  z  n   =    k −  ∑  j = 1   k − 1   ( k − j )  P  j    z  j     1 −  ∑  j = 1   k    P  j    z  j      .   {\displaystyle G_{P_{1},\ldots ,P_{k}}(z)=\sum _{n=0}^{\infty }V_{n}(P_{1},\ldots ,P_{k})z^{n}={\frac {k-\sum _{j=1}^{k-1}(k-j)P_{j}z^{j}}{1-\sum _{j=1}^{k}P_{j}z^{j}}}.}

# Lucas sequence

 [Edit links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q1759646#sitelinks-wikipedia)                          From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia   Certain constant-recursive integer sequences Not to be confused with the sequence of [Lucas numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_number), which is a particular Lucas sequence.

In [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), the **Lucas sequences**      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}   are certain [constant-recursive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constant-recursive_sequence) [integer sequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_sequence) that satisfy the [recurrence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrence_relation)

      x  n   = P ⋅  x  n − 1   − Q ⋅  x  n − 2     {\displaystyle x_{n}=P\cdot x_{n-1}-Q\cdot x_{n-2}}

where     P   {\displaystyle P}   and     Q   {\displaystyle Q}   are fixed [integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer). Although      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}   satisfy the same recurrence relation, they differ on the values of their first two elements and thus differ for subsequent elements as well. Any sequence satisfying this recurrence relation can be represented as a [linear combination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_combination) of the Lucas sequences      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q ) .   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q).}

More generally, Lucas sequences      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}   represent sequences of [polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial) in     P   {\displaystyle P}   and     Q   {\displaystyle Q}   with integer [coefficients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coefficient).

Famous examples of Lucas sequences include the [Fibonacci numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_number), [Mersenne numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mersenne_number), [Pell numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell_number), [Lucas numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_number), [Jacobsthal numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobsthal_number), and a superset of [Fermat numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_number) (see below). Lucas sequences are named after the [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France) mathematician [Édouard Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89douard_Lucas).

Recurrence relations

# Recurrence relations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=1)]

Given two integer parameters     P   {\displaystyle P}   and     Q   {\displaystyle Q}  , the Lucas sequences of the first kind      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and of the second kind      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}   are defined by the [recurrence relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrence_relation):

          U  0   ( P , Q )    = 0 ,      U  1   ( P , Q )    = 1 ,      U  n   ( P , Q )    = P ⋅  U  n − 1   ( P , Q ) − Q ⋅  U  n − 2   ( P , Q )    for    n > 1 ,       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}U_{0}(P,Q)&=0,\\U_{1}(P,Q)&=1,\\U_{n}(P,Q)&=P\cdot U_{n-1}(P,Q)-Q\cdot U_{n-2}(P,Q){\mbox{ for }}n>1,\end{aligned}}}

and

          V  0   ( P , Q )    = 2 ,      V  1   ( P , Q )    = P ,      V  n   ( P , Q )    = P ⋅  V  n − 1   ( P , Q ) − Q ⋅  V  n − 2   ( P , Q )    for    n > 1.       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}V_{0}(P,Q)&=2,\\V_{1}(P,Q)&=P,\\V_{n}(P,Q)&=P\cdot V_{n-1}(P,Q)-Q\cdot V_{n-2}(P,Q){\mbox{ for }}n>1.\end{aligned}}}

It is not hard to show that for     n > 0   {\displaystyle n>0}  ,

          U  n   ( P , Q )    =    P ⋅  U  n − 1   ( P , Q ) +  V  n − 1   ( P , Q )  2   ,      V  n   ( P , Q )    =    (  P  2   − 4 Q ) ⋅  U  n − 1   ( P , Q ) + P ⋅  V  n − 1   ( P , Q )  2   .       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}U_{n}(P,Q)&={\frac {P\cdot U_{n-1}(P,Q)+V_{n-1}(P,Q)}{2}},\\V_{n}(P,Q)&={\frac {(P^{2}-4Q)\cdot U_{n-1}(P,Q)+P\cdot V_{n-1}(P,Q)}{2}}.\end{aligned}}}

The above relations can be stated in [matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) form as follows:

       [     U  n   ( P , Q )      U  n + 1   ( P , Q )    ]   =   [    0   1     − Q   P    ]   ⋅   [     U  n − 1   ( P , Q )      U  n   ( P , Q )    ]   ,   {\displaystyle {\begin{bmatrix}U_{n}(P,Q)\\U_{n+1}(P,Q)\end{bmatrix}}={\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-Q&P\end{bmatrix}}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}U_{n-1}(P,Q)\\U_{n}(P,Q)\end{bmatrix}},}

       [     V  n   ( P , Q )      V  n + 1   ( P , Q )    ]   =   [    0   1     − Q   P    ]   ⋅   [     V  n − 1   ( P , Q )      V  n   ( P , Q )    ]   ,   {\displaystyle {\begin{bmatrix}V_{n}(P,Q)\\V_{n+1}(P,Q)\end{bmatrix}}={\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-Q&P\end{bmatrix}}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}V_{n-1}(P,Q)\\V_{n}(P,Q)\end{bmatrix}},}

       [     U  n   ( P , Q )      V  n   ( P , Q )    ]   =   [    P  /  2   1  /  2     (  P  2   − 4 Q )  /  2   P  /  2    ]   ⋅   [     U  n − 1   ( P , Q )      V  n − 1   ( P , Q )    ]   .   {\displaystyle {\begin{bmatrix}U_{n}(P,Q)\\V_{n}(P,Q)\end{bmatrix}}={\begin{bmatrix}P/2&1/2\\(P^{2}-4Q)/2&P/2\end{bmatrix}}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}U_{n-1}(P,Q)\\V_{n-1}(P,Q)\end{bmatrix}}.}

Initial terms of Lucas sequences      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}   are given in the table:

         n    U  n   ( P , Q )    V  n   ( P , Q )     0   0   2     1   1   P     2   P     P   2   − 2 Q     3     P   2   − Q     P   3   − 3 P Q     4     P   3   − 2 P Q     P   4   − 4   P   2   Q + 2   Q   2       5     P   4   − 3   P   2   Q +   Q   2       P   5   − 5   P   3   Q + 5 P   Q   2       6     P   5   − 4   P   3   Q + 3 P   Q   2       P   6   − 6   P   4   Q + 9   P   2     Q   2   − 2   Q   3         {\displaystyle {\begin{array}{r|l|l}n&U_{n}(P,Q)&V_{n}(P,Q)\\\hline 0&0&2\\1&1&P\\2&P&{P}^{2}-2Q\\3&{P}^{2}-Q&{P}^{3}-3PQ\\4&{P}^{3}-2PQ&{P}^{4}-4{P}^{2}Q+2{Q}^{2}\\5&{P}^{4}-3{P}^{2}Q+{Q}^{2}&{P}^{5}-5{P}^{3}Q+5P{Q}^{2}\\6&{P}^{5}-4{P}^{3}Q+3P{Q}^{2}&{P}^{6}-6{P}^{4}Q+9{P}^{2}{Q}^{2}-2{Q}^{3}\end{array}}}

Explicit expressions

# Explicit expressions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=2)]

The characteristic equation of the recurrence relation for Lucas sequences      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}   is:

      x  2   − P x + Q = 0    {\displaystyle x^{2}-Px+Q=0\,}

It has the [discriminant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discriminant)     D =  P  2   − 4 Q   {\displaystyle D=P^{2}-4Q}   and, by the [quadratic formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_formula), has the [roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_of_a_polynomial):

     a =    P +   D    2     and   b =    P −   D    2   .    {\displaystyle a={\frac {P+{\sqrt {D}}}{2}}\quad {\text{and}}\quad b={\frac {P-{\sqrt {D}}}{2}}.\,}

Thus:

     a + b = P  ,   {\displaystyle a+b=P\,,}       a b =   1 4   (  P  2   − D ) = Q  ,   {\displaystyle ab={\frac {1}{4}}(P^{2}-D)=Q\,,}       a − b =   D    .   {\displaystyle a-b={\sqrt {D}}\,.}

Note that the sequence      a  n     {\displaystyle a^{n}}   and the sequence      b  n     {\displaystyle b^{n}}   also satisfy the recurrence relation. However these might not be integer sequences.

Distinct roots

# Distinct roots

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=3)]

When     D ≠ 0   {\displaystyle D\neq 0}  , *a* and *b* are distinct and one quickly verifies that

      a  n   =     V  n   +  U  n     D    2     {\displaystyle a^{n}={\frac {V_{n}+U_{n}{\sqrt {D}}}{2}}}        b  n   =     V  n   −  U  n     D    2   .   {\displaystyle b^{n}={\frac {V_{n}-U_{n}{\sqrt {D}}}{2}}.}

It follows that the terms of Lucas sequences can be expressed in terms of *a* and *b* as follows

      U  n   =     a  n   −  b  n     a − b    =     a  n   −  b  n     D      {\displaystyle U_{n}={\frac {a^{n}-b^{n}}{a-b}}={\frac {a^{n}-b^{n}}{\sqrt {D}}}}        V  n   =  a  n   +  b  n      {\displaystyle V_{n}=a^{n}+b^{n}\,}

Repeated root

# Repeated root

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=4)]

The case     D = 0   {\displaystyle D=0}   occurs exactly when     P = 2 S   and   Q =  S  2     {\displaystyle P=2S{\text{ and }}Q=S^{2}}   for some integer *S* so that     a = b = S   {\displaystyle a=b=S}  . In this case one easily finds that

      U  n   ( P , Q ) =  U  n   ( 2 S ,  S  2   ) = n  S  n − 1      {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)=U_{n}(2S,S^{2})=nS^{n-1}\,}        V  n   ( P , Q ) =  V  n   ( 2 S ,  S  2   ) = 2  S  n   .    {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)=V_{n}(2S,S^{2})=2S^{n}.\,}

Properties

# Properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=5)]

Generating functions

# Generating functions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=6)]

The ordinary [generating functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generating_function) are

      ∑  n ≥ 0    U  n   ( P , Q )  z  n   =   z  1 − P z + Q  z  2      ;   {\displaystyle \sum _{n\geq 0}U_{n}(P,Q)z^{n}={\frac {z}{1-Pz+Qz^{2}}};}        ∑  n ≥ 0    V  n   ( P , Q )  z  n   =    2 − P z   1 − P z + Q  z  2      .   {\displaystyle \sum _{n\geq 0}V_{n}(P,Q)z^{n}={\frac {2-Pz}{1-Pz+Qz^{2}}}.}

Pell equations

# Pell equations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=7)]

When     Q = ± 1   {\displaystyle Q=\pm 1}  , the Lucas sequences      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}   satisfy certain [Pell equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell_equation):

      V  n   ( P , 1  )  2   − D ⋅  U  n   ( P , 1  )  2   = 4 ,   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,1)^{2}-D\cdot U_{n}(P,1)^{2}=4,}        V  n   ( P , − 1  )  2   − D ⋅  U  n   ( P , − 1  )  2   = 4 ( − 1  )  n   .   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,-1)^{2}-D\cdot U_{n}(P,-1)^{2}=4(-1)^{n}.}

Relations between sequences with different parameters

# Relations between sequences with different parameters

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=8)]
- For any number *c*, the sequences      U  n   (  P ′  ,  Q ′  )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P',Q')}   and      V  n   (  P ′  ,  Q ′  )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P',Q')}   with
      P ′  = P + 2 c   {\displaystyle P'=P+2c}        Q ′  = c P + Q +  c  2     {\displaystyle Q'=cP+Q+c^{2}}   have the same discriminant as      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}  :      P  ′  2    − 4  Q ′  = ( P + 2 c  )  2   − 4 ( c P + Q +  c  2   ) =  P  2   − 4 Q = D .   {\displaystyle P'^{2}-4Q'=(P+2c)^{2}-4(cP+Q+c^{2})=P^{2}-4Q=D.}
- For any number *c*, we also have
      U  n   ( c P ,  c  2   Q ) =  c  n − 1   ⋅  U  n   ( P , Q ) ,   {\displaystyle U_{n}(cP,c^{2}Q)=c^{n-1}\cdot U_{n}(P,Q),}        V  n   ( c P ,  c  2   Q ) =  c  n   ⋅  V  n   ( P , Q ) .   {\displaystyle V_{n}(cP,c^{2}Q)=c^{n}\cdot V_{n}(P,Q).}

#### Fast computation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=10)]

Various analogues of [exponentiation by squaring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponentiation_by_squaring) can be used to calculate Lucas sequences efficiently, in ⁠      O   ( log ⁡ n )   {\displaystyle {\mathcal {O}}(\log n)}  ⁠ operations. To simultaneously calculate      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}  , one can use the properties (3) and (4) to perform double-and-add. Alternatively, calculate the matrix exponentiation      M  n   =   (        0   1     − Q   P        )     {\displaystyle M^{n}={\big (}{\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-Q&P\end{smallmatrix}}{\big )}}   to use       (          U  n          U  n + 1           )   =  M  n     (        0     1        )     {\displaystyle {\big (}{\begin{smallmatrix}{U_{n}}\\{U_{n+1}}\end{smallmatrix}}{\big )}=M^{n}{\big (}{\begin{smallmatrix}0\\1\end{smallmatrix}}{\big )}}   and       (          V  n          V  n + 1           )   =  M  n     (        2     P        )   .   {\displaystyle {\big (}{\begin{smallmatrix}{V_{n}}\\{V_{n+1}}\end{smallmatrix}}{\big )}=M^{n}{\big (}{\begin{smallmatrix}2\\P\end{smallmatrix}}{\big )}.}

(6) and (7) allow fast calculation of *V* independent of *U* using double-and-add. The relation      V  m n   =  V  m   ( P =  V  n   , Q =  Q  n   )   {\displaystyle V_{mn}=V_{m}(P=V_{n},Q=Q_{n})}   (which belongs to the section above, "relations between sequences with different parameters") is also useful for this purpose.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-1)

Another ⁠      O   ( log ⁡ n )   {\displaystyle {\mathcal {O}}(\log n)}  ⁠ method based on (3) and (6) is the [Lucas chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_chain). This method takes fewer operations than double-and-add but requires pre-calculation of chains.

Divisibility properties

# Divisibility properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=11)]

Among the consequences is that      U  k m   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{km}(P,Q)}   is a multiple of      U  m   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{m}(P,Q)}  , i.e., the sequence     (  U  m   ( P , Q )  )  m ≥ 1     {\displaystyle (U_{m}(P,Q))_{m\geq 1}}   is a [divisibility sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisibility_sequence). This implies, in particular, that      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   can be [prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number) only when *n* is prime. Moreover, if     gcd ( P , Q ) = 1   {\displaystyle \gcd(P,Q)=1}  , then     (  U  m   ( P , Q )  )  m ≥ 1     {\displaystyle (U_{m}(P,Q))_{m\geq 1}}   is a [strong divisibility sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisibility_sequence).

Other divisibility properties are as follows:[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-2)

- If *n* is an [odd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parity_(mathematics)) multiple of *m*, then      V  m     {\displaystyle V_{m}}   divides      V  n     {\displaystyle V_{n}}  .
- Let *N* be an integer [relatively prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relatively_prime) to 2*Q*. If the smallest positive integer *r* for which *N* divides      U  r     {\displaystyle U_{r}}   exists, then the set of *n* for which *N* divides      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   is exactly the set of multiples of *r*.
- If *P* and *Q* are [even](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parity_(mathematics)), then      U  n   ,  V  n     {\displaystyle U_{n},V_{n}}   are always even except      U  1     {\displaystyle U_{1}}  .
- If *P* is odd and *Q* is even, then      U  n   ,  V  n     {\displaystyle U_{n},V_{n}}   are always odd for every     n > 0   {\displaystyle n>0}  .
- If *P* is even and *Q* is odd, then the [parity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parity_(mathematics)) of      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   is the same as *n* and      V  n     {\displaystyle V_{n}}   is always even.
- If *P* and *Q* are odd, then      U  n   ,  V  n     {\displaystyle U_{n},V_{n}}   are even if and only if *n* is a multiple of 3.
- If *p* is an odd prime, then      U  p   ≡  (    D p    )  ,  V  p   ≡ P   ( mod  p )    {\displaystyle U_{p}\equiv \left({\tfrac {D}{p}}\right),V_{p}\equiv P{\pmod {p}}}   (see [Legendre symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre_symbol)).
- If *p* is an odd prime which divides *P* and *Q*, then *p* divides      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   for every     n > 1   {\displaystyle n>1}  .
- If *p* is an odd prime which divides *P* but not *Q*, then *p* divides      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   if and only if *n* is even.
- If *p* is an odd prime which divides *Q* but not *P*, then *p* never divides      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   for any     n > 0   {\displaystyle n>0}  .
- If *p* is an odd prime which divides *D* but not *PQ*, then *p* divides      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   if and only if *p* divides *n*.
- If *p* is an odd prime which does not divide *PQD*, then *p* divides      U  l     {\displaystyle U_{l}}  , where     l = p −  (    D p    )    {\displaystyle l=p-\left({\tfrac {D}{p}}\right)}  .

The last fact generalizes [Fermat's little theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat's_little_theorem). These facts are used in the [Lucas–Lehmer primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas%E2%80%93Lehmer_primality_test). Like Fermat's little theorem, the [converse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Converse_(logic)) of the last fact holds often, but not always; there exist [composite numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_number) *n* relatively prime to *D* and dividing      U  l     {\displaystyle U_{l}}  , where     l = n −  (    D n    )    {\displaystyle l=n-\left({\tfrac {D}{n}}\right)}  . Such composite numbers are called [Lucas pseudoprimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_pseudoprime).

A [prime factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_factor) of a term in a Lucas sequence which does not divide any earlier term in the sequence is called **primitive**. [Carmichael's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael's_theorem) states that all but finitely many of the terms in a Lucas sequence have a primitive prime factor.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-Yabuta-3) Indeed, [Carmichael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Daniel_Carmichael) (1913) showed that if *D* is positive and *n* is not 1, 2 or 6, then      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   has a primitive prime factor. In the case *D* is negative, a deep result of Bilu, Hanrot, Voutier and Mignotte[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-4) shows that if *n* > 30, then      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   has a primitive prime factor and determines all cases      U  n     {\displaystyle U_{n}}   has no primitive prime factor.

Specific names

# Specific names

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=12)]

The Lucas sequences for some values of *P* and *Q* have specific names:

 *Un*(1, −1) : [Fibonacci numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_number) *Vn*(1, −1) : [Lucas numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_number) *Un*(2, −1) : [Pell numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell_number) *Vn*(2, −1) : [Pell–Lucas numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell%E2%80%93Lucas_numbers) (companion Pell numbers) *Un*(2, 1) : [Counting numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counting_numbers) *Un*(1, −2) : [Jacobsthal numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobsthal_number) *Vn*(1, −2) : [Jacobsthal–Lucas numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobsthal%E2%80%93Lucas_numbers) *Un*(3, 2) : [Mersenne numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mersenne_number) 2*n* − 1 *Vn*(3, 2) : Numbers of the form 2*n* + 1, which include the [Fermat numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_number)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-Yabuta-3) *Un*(6, 1) : The square roots of the [square triangular numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_triangular_number). *Un*(*x*, −1) : [Fibonacci polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_polynomials) *Vn*(*x*, −1) : [Lucas polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_polynomials) *Un*(2*x*, 1) : [Chebyshev polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebyshev_polynomials) of second kind *Vn*(2*x*, 1) : [Chebyshev polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebyshev_polynomials) of first kind multiplied by 2 *Un*(*x* + 1, *x*) : [Repunits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repunit) in base *x* *Vn*(*x* + 1, *x*) : *x**n* + 1

Applications

# Applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=13)]
- Lucas sequences are used in probabilistic [Lucas pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_pseudoprime) tests, which are part of the commonly used [Baillie–PSW primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baillie%E2%80%93PSW_primality_test).
- Lucas sequences are used in some primality proof methods, including the [Lucas–Lehmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas%E2%80%93Lehmer_primality_test) and [Lucas–Lehmer–Riesel tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas%E2%80%93Lehmer%E2%80%93Riesel_test) and the hybrid N−1/N+1 methods such as those in Brillhart-Lehmer-Selfridge 1975.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-BLS75-6)
- LUC is a [public-key cryptosystem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public-key_cryptosystem) based on Lucas sequences[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-7) that implements the analogs of [ElGamal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ElGamal) (LUCELG), [Diffie–Hellman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffie%E2%80%93Hellman) (LUCDIF), and [RSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(algorithm)) (LUCRSA). The encryption of the message in LUC is computed as a term of certain Lucas sequence, instead of using [modular exponentiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_exponentiation) as in RSA or Diffie–Hellman. However, it is argued[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence#cite_note-8) that many of the supposed security advantages of LUC over cryptosystems based on modular exponentiation are either not present, or not as substantial as claimed.

Generalizations

# Generalizations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lucas_sequence&action=edit&section=14)]

The sequence      V  n   ( P , Q ) =  a  n   +  b  n     {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)=a^{n}+b^{n}}  , which is a solution to the recurrence      V  n   ( P , Q ) = P  V  n − 1   ( P , Q ) − Q  V  n − 2   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)=PV_{n-1}(P,Q)-QV_{n-2}(P,Q)}   when ⁠    a   {\displaystyle a}  ⁠ and ⁠    b   {\displaystyle b}  ⁠ are the roots of the corresponding quadratic equation ⁠     z  2   − P z + Q = 0   {\displaystyle z^{2}-Pz+Q=0}  ⁠, generalizes to degree ⁠    k ≥ 1   {\displaystyle k\geq 1}  ⁠. Specifically, for the recurrence relation      V  n   (  P  1   , … ,  P  k   ) =  ∑  j = 1   k    P  j    V  n − j   (  P  1   , … ,  P  k   )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P_{1},\ldots ,P_{k})=\sum _{j=1}^{k}P_{j}V_{n-j}(P_{1},\ldots ,P_{k})}   with integers ⁠     P  1   , … ,  P  k     {\displaystyle P_{1},\ldots ,P_{k}}  ⁠ and typically with ⁠     P  k   ≠ 0   {\displaystyle P_{k}\neq 0}  ⁠, let ⁠     a  1   , … ,  a  k     {\displaystyle a_{1},\ldots ,a_{k}}  ⁠ be the roots of the corresponding polynomial equation      z  k   −  ∑  j = 1   k    P  j    z  k − j   = 0.   {\displaystyle z^{k}-\sum _{j=1}^{k}P_{j}z^{k-j}=0.}   Then      V  n   (  P  1   , … ,  P  k   ) =  ∑  j = 1   k    a  j   n     {\displaystyle V_{n}(P_{1},\ldots ,P_{k})=\sum _{j=1}^{k}a_{j}^{n}}   is a sequence of integers satisfying the recurrence, as is evidenced by its [ordinary generating function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinary_generating_function),      G   P  1   , … ,  P  k     ( z ) =  ∑  n = 0   ∞    V  n   (  P  1   , … ,  P  k   )  z  n   =    k −  ∑  j = 1   k − 1   ( k − j )  P  j    z  j     1 −  ∑  j = 1   k    P  j    z  j      .   {\displaystyle G_{P_{1},\ldots ,P_{k}}(z)=\sum _{n=0}^{\infty }V_{n}(P_{1},\ldots ,P_{k})z^{n}={\frac {k-\sum _{j=1}^{k-1}(k-j)P_{j}z^{j}}{1-\sum _{j=1}^{k}P_{j}z^{j}}}.}
